slides.title: What Are Access Modifiers?
slides.content: Access modifiers control the visibility and accessibility of your code members (fields, methods, properties, etc.). They define who can read or call a member, helping you enforce encapsulation.
slides.example:
public class Person
{
    private string secret;       // only within Person
    public string Name;          // anyone
    protected int Age;           // Person + derived classes
    internal string Email;       // same assembly
}
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: What is the primary purpose of access modifiers?
options: To control the visibility and accessibility of members
exercise.answer: To control the visibility and accessibility of members

slides.title: public vs private
slides.content: 'public' means the member is accessible from anywhere—inside the class, in derived classes, in other assemblies. 'private' means it is accessible only within the containing class, providing the strongest encapsulation.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Which modifier would you use for the 'balance' field to hide it from other classes?

slides.title: protected
slides.content: 'protected' members are accessible within the containing class and within any class that derives from it. This is key for inheritance—you expose data to subclasses but not to unrelated external code.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition with a method that writes to the console; produces no output unless the method is invoked.

exercise.prompt: A _____ member is accessible in the containing class and derived classes, but not in unrelated classes.

slides.title: internal
slides.content: 'internal' means a member is accessible from anywhere within the same assembly (the compiled DLL or EXE). External assemblies cannot access it. This is useful for exposing APIs to your own library without exposing them publicly.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

slides.title: protected internal and private protected
slides.content: 'protected internal' means accessible from the same assembly OR from derived classes (even in other assemblies) — a logical OR. 'private protected' means accessible only from within the same assembly AND only from derived classes within that assembly.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

slides.title: Default Access Modifiers
slides.content: When you omit an access modifier, types default to 'internal' and class members default to 'private'. It is always best practice to explicitly specify the modifier rather than relying on defaults.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: A top-level class with no access modifier defaults to ______.

slides.title: Access Modifiers in Inheritance
slides.content: When inheriting from a class, you can access public, protected, internal, and protected internal members—but never private members. Private members are invisible to derived classes.

slides.title: Best Practices and Assemblies
slides.content: Use the most restrictive modifier that still allows your code to work. Mark classes 'internal' by default unless you need them public. Keep fields 'private' and expose them through 'public' properties for validation and control.

exercise.answer: Use the most restrictive modifier that still allows the code to work
